title: Four of Pentacles — Keep What You Need, and Leave Room to Move

quickTake.upright: Decide what is worth keeping and establish boundaries that help you feel secure.
quickTake.reversed: Holding too tightly brings life to a halt, or loosening a boundary makes it hard to restore.

hook: The figure in the Four of Pentacles places all four discs against his body: one above his head, one at his chest, and two under his feet. The possessions seem safe. But if he wants to stand up, what must he do first?

sections.title: The body becomes a stand for guarding the pentacles
sections.bodyMarkdown:
A crowned figure sits facing us on a stone seat, wearing a red robe and a dark outer garment. His arms encircle the large pentacle at his chest, another stands on his crown, and each foot rests on a third or fourth disc. The discs occupy his head, hands, and feet, forming a tightly arranged vertical composition.

A city spreads out behind him, with towers, walls, and red roofs, yet he sits in an open space in front of it, interacting with no one. What we can see is stillness and a firm embrace. “Fear of loss” is an interpretation suggested by that posture, not a fact established by reading his mind. [View the card used in this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pents04.jpg)

sections.title: What is protected also occupies the body
sections.bodyMarkdown:
The four pentacles connect the top of his head, his hands, and his feet. This position can be very steady, but leaves almost nothing free to reach for anything else. There is no need to blame the figure as soon as you look at the image. First acknowledge that safekeeping has a purpose, then notice how much freedom of movement it costs him. The city stands just behind him, yet plays no part in what he is doing: a clue for discussing resources and distance from other people.

The Two of Pentacles responds to change through movement; the Four creates security through limits. Neither is simply good or bad: too much activity may call for protection, while too much protection may need adjusting. Judge the difference through the present circumstances. Do not treat every refusal as shutting people out, or present every form of control as responsibility.

sections.title: Holding on has direct support in the text
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Waite briefly describes the figure as keeping what he possesses. His upright meanings concern secure possessions, attachment to what one has, and older meanings involving gifts and inheritance. Reversed, he gives suspense, delay, and opposition, rather than directly equating the card with the modern idea of “letting go.”

This article extends the idea of preserving what one has to time, permissions, belongings, and personal boundaries. Reversal is used to examine whether boundaries are too tight or too loose. This is a contemporary reflective method, not a rewritten version of the old list presented as the original text. [Check Waite’s text](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktpe04.htm)

sections.title: Upright: preserve what really matters
sections.bodyMarkdown:
The upright card need not immediately be judged as stinginess. During a period of change, keeping a familiar space, reducing additional commitments, or giving important belongings a fixed place can all provide practical stability. Ask what you are protecting before deciding whether the boundary is appropriate.

A useful boundary can be explained and adjusted. For example, you might reserve a daily period when you take on no new tasks, while agreeing how to make contact in an emergency. It protects your ability to keep living your life; it need not close off every form of contact.

sections.title: Reversed: notice the cost of control
sections.bodyMarkdown:
If fear of mistakes means everything must pass through you, safekeeping can become a bottleneck. You retain the authority to decide but lose room for rest and collaboration. First distinguish responsibilities that truly cannot be handed over from parts others could manage under clear rules.

Another possibility is suddenly accepting requests beyond your capacity to avoid appearing ungenerous. Letting go also needs limits: when borrowed items must be returned, or how far permission to use your materials extends. Clear communication offers more stability than alternating between locking everything down and opening everything up.

sections.title: How protection and circulation can coexist
sections.bodyMarkdown:
A team leader can begin by handing over one low-risk task and agreeing on a checkpoint, to practise allowing others to take responsibility. When sorting your own possessions, separate useful things, keepsakes, and things that “might be useful someday,” then decide on each in turn.

In a relationship, you can state directly when you need time alone and why. Using silence or repeated tests to ensure the other person will not leave may create a sense of control without bringing real reassurance.

sections.title: Case one: an explainable boundary around creative time
sections.bodyMarkdown:
An original fictional case. Xiaocheng plans to finish her portfolio in six weeks and has already set aside two evenings a week to organise her work. Yet friends and family regularly ask her that same day for help editing photos. She does not want to distance herself from them and keeps agreeing, so her own plans repeatedly fall through. The Four of Pentacles appears upright in the advice position. Her question is: “How can I protect the time after work that I need to prepare my portfolio?”

The disc held against the chest can correspond to the limited time she has clearly identified as worth protecting; the two beneath the feet suggest that stability needs concrete foundations. This does not ask her to refuse everyone. It first asks that existing arrangements stop being available for reassignment at any moment. She tells friends and family that she will not take on last-minute photo editing on those two evenings. At other times, she will check the amount of work before deciding whether to accept.

If the portfolio schedule itself turns out to be so full that it consumes all her spare time, the boundary may need redesigning rather than treating everyone close to her as an interruption. Each week, she checks what she has actually completed and whether she still gets basic rest, while leaving a way to reach her for genuine emergencies. Upright “holding on” takes the form of arrangements with a purpose and defined limits; repeatedly telling herself to be more disciplined is not enough.

sections.title: Case two: only one person holds the storeroom key
sections.bodyMarkdown:
An original fictional case. A community lending shelf holds ladders, trolleys, and tools. Its coordinator worries that items will be lost, so every loan must wait until he finishes work and opens the door. He asks for nothing in return, but four people have already given up borrowing in one week because the times did not fit. Asked “Why do the items on our mutual-aid shelf so rarely get borrowed?”, the Four of Pentacles appears reversed in the obstacle position.

Starting from the tight embrace of the pentacle and the feet pressing down on two more, the interpretation of safekeeping becoming a bottleneck fits the facts. The objects are protected, but the purpose of the shelf cannot be fulfilled. There is no need to accuse the coordinator of stinginess. His concerns are real, and any change should retain the necessary management.

He first selects low-risk items that are easy to check and, with another volunteer, trials a register for loans and returns, clarifying how to report damage. If there really have been repeated losses without records of responsibility, they should establish those records before expanding access. After the trial, they check both whether borrowing is convenient and whether items come back as agreed. Seeking only to “let go” while leaving no one responsible would take them to the other extreme of this reversed reading.

sections.title: Exercise: give a boundary a reason
sections.bodyMarkdown: Complete these sentences: “What I want to keep is … because it helps me …” and “What I can make available is … provided that …” If the only reason left is “I must control everything,” look again for a more specific need that can be discussed.

sections.title: Common misreadings
sections.bodyMarkdown: The Four of Pentacles cannot label someone a miser on the strength of one card, nor does it demand that you immediately discard or hand over all your belongings. The focus is whether the boundary supports real needs and whether the cost of maintaining it remains manageable.

sections.title: Tightening and loosening both need a reason
sections.bodyMarkdown: Reversal can raise the question of excessive restriction, or of suddenly removing every boundary. To distinguish them, ask what has happened recently: does every task get stuck awaiting approval, or have too many promises already been made and become difficult to withdraw? Without facts, the same image cannot choose the answer for you. Especially where shared property, materials, and privacy are involved, changes to access require the explicit agreement of those concerned. A card’s symbolism cannot replace permission.

# Four of Pentacles — Keep What You Need, and Leave Room to Move

The figure in the Four of Pentacles places all four discs against his body: one above his head, one at his chest, and two under his feet. The possessions seem safe. But if he wants to stand up, what must he do first?

## The body becomes a stand for guarding the pentacles

A crowned figure sits facing us on a stone seat, wearing a red robe and a dark outer garment. His arms encircle the large pentacle at his chest, another stands on his crown, and each foot rests on a third or fourth disc. A city spreads out behind him, with towers, walls, and red roofs, yet he sits in an open space in front of it, interacting with no one. What we can see is stillness and a firm embrace. “Fear of loss” is an interpretation suggested by that posture, not a fact established by reading his mind. [View the card used in this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pents04.jpg)

## What is protected also occupies the body

The four pentacles connect the top of his head, his hands, and his feet. This position can be very steady, but leaves almost nothing free to reach for anything else. There is no need to blame the figure as soon as you look at the image. First acknowledge that safekeeping has a purpose, then notice how much freedom of movement it costs him. The city stands just behind him, yet plays no part in what he is doing: a clue for discussing resources and distance from other people.

The Two of Pentacles responds to change through movement; the Four creates security through limits. Neither is simply good or bad: too much activity may call for protection, while too much protection may need adjusting. Judge the difference through the present circumstances. Do not treat every refusal as shutting people out, or present every form of control as responsibility.

## Holding on has direct support in the text

Waite briefly describes the figure as keeping what he possesses. His upright meanings concern secure possessions, attachment to what one has, and older meanings involving gifts and inheritance. Reversed, he gives suspense, delay, and opposition, rather than directly equating the card with the modern idea of “letting go.”

This article extends the idea of preserving what one has to time, permissions, belongings, and personal boundaries. Reversal is used to examine whether boundaries are too tight or too loose. This is a contemporary reflective method, not a rewritten version of the old list presented as the original text. [Check Waite’s text](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktpe04.htm)

## Upright: preserve what really matters

The upright card need not immediately be judged as stinginess. During a period of change, keeping a familiar space, reducing additional commitments, or giving important belongings a fixed place can all provide practical stability. Ask what you are protecting before deciding whether the boundary is appropriate.

A useful boundary can be explained and adjusted. For example, you might reserve a daily period when you take on no new tasks, while agreeing how to make contact in an emergency. It protects your ability to keep living your life; it need not close off every form of contact.

## Reversed: notice the cost of control

If fear of mistakes means everything must pass through you, safekeeping can become a bottleneck. You retain the authority to decide but lose room for rest and collaboration. First distinguish responsibilities that truly cannot be handed over from parts others could manage under clear rules.

Another possibility is suddenly accepting requests beyond your capacity to avoid appearing ungenerous. Letting go also needs limits: when borrowed items must be returned, or how far permission to use your materials extends. Clear communication offers more stability than alternating between locking everything down and opening everything up.

## How protection and circulation can coexist

A team leader can begin by handing over one low-risk task and agreeing on a checkpoint, to practise allowing others to take responsibility. When sorting your own possessions, separate useful things, keepsakes, and things that “might be useful someday,” then decide on each in turn.

In a relationship, you can state directly when you need time alone and why. Using silence or repeated tests to ensure the other person will not leave may create a sense of control without bringing real reassurance.

## Case one: an explainable boundary around creative time

An original fictional case. Xiaocheng plans to finish her portfolio in six weeks and has already set aside two evenings a week to organise her work. Yet friends and family regularly ask her that same day for help editing photos. She does not want to distance herself from them and keeps agreeing, so her own plans repeatedly fall through. The Four of Pentacles appears upright in the advice position. Her question is: “How can I protect the time after work that I need to prepare my portfolio?”

The disc held against the chest can correspond to the limited time she has clearly identified as worth protecting; the two beneath the feet suggest that stability needs concrete foundations. This does not ask her to refuse everyone. It first asks that existing arrangements stop being available for reassignment at any moment. She tells friends and family that she will not take on last-minute photo editing on those two evenings. At other times, she will check the amount of work before deciding whether to accept.

If the portfolio schedule itself turns out to be so full that it consumes all her spare time, the boundary may need redesigning rather than treating everyone close to her as an interruption. Each week, she checks what she has actually completed and whether she still gets basic rest, while leaving a way to reach her for genuine emergencies. Upright “holding on” takes the form of arrangements with a purpose and defined limits; repeatedly telling herself to be more disciplined is not enough.

## Case two: only one person holds the storeroom key

An original fictional case. A community lending shelf holds ladders, trolleys, and tools. Its coordinator worries that items will be lost, so every loan must wait until he finishes work and opens the door. He asks for nothing in return, but four people have already given up borrowing in one week because the times did not fit. Asked “Why do the items on our mutual-aid shelf so rarely get borrowed?”, the Four of Pentacles appears reversed in the obstacle position.

Starting from the tight embrace of the pentacle and the feet pressing down on two more, the interpretation of safekeeping becoming a bottleneck fits the facts. The objects are protected, but the purpose of the shelf cannot be fulfilled. There is no need to accuse the coordinator of stinginess. His concerns are real, and any change should retain the necessary management.

He first selects low-risk items that are easy to check and, with another volunteer, trials a register for loans and returns, clarifying how to report damage. After the trial, they check both whether borrowing is convenient and whether items come back as agreed. Seeking only to “let go” while leaving no one responsible would take them to the other extreme of this reversed reading.

## Exercise: give a boundary a reason

Complete these sentences: “What I want to keep is … because it helps me …” and “What I can make available is … provided that …” If the only reason left is “I must control everything,” look again for a more specific need that can be discussed.

## Common misreadings

The Four of Pentacles cannot label someone a miser on the strength of one card, nor does it demand that you immediately discard or hand over all your belongings. The focus is whether the boundary supports real needs and whether the cost of maintaining it remains manageable.

## Tightening and loosening both need a reason

Reversal can raise the question of excessive restriction, or of suddenly removing every boundary. To distinguish them, ask what has happened recently: does every task get stuck awaiting approval, or have too many promises already been made and become difficult to withdraw? Without facts, the same image cannot choose the answer for you. Especially where shared property, materials, and privacy are involved, changes to access require the explicit agreement of those concerned. A card’s symbolism cannot replace permission.

Waite’s *The Pictorial Key to the Tarot*, cross-checked against the [complete English text](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_3). Directly visible imagery, historical divinatory meanings, and modern reflective applications are distinguished here. Both cases are original fiction, not empirical evidence of divination’s accuracy.
